name: Uma Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Uma. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at half four and on the Pryce farm by five for the first milking, sixty-odd cows in a herringbone parlour that's older than me. After that it's calves, scraping out, and whatever Gwen Pryce has on her list, mending fence on the top fields or loading straw. I've only been at it three years, since the bakery in town shut, so I'm still the one who gets told twice how to set the cluster on a kicker.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the calves, honestly, and being outside instead of under strip lights wrapping loaves. What wears me out is the hours and my back, and knowing I'm forty-three and still the slowest pair of hands in the yard. My partner Tom drives the school bus, so between us we just about cover the mortgage, and our two, Maisie and Owen, think I smell of cow permanently.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let the tech people have their bubble and leave us alone. Down the pub I'd probably say the only thing AI ever did for a farm was the weather app getting it wrong. I don't post online, I haven't got the time or the patience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully it means my life stays as hard as it already is. Nobody needs a computer to make milking at five in the morning any worse; milk prices and the bank manage that fine on their own. The Pryces are always one bad winter from selling the herd.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep turning up, same as now, and keep putting forty pounds a week into the tin like Tom and I agreed. I'd go to the farmworkers' union meeting in town that I keep missing, because if the Pryces ever do sell, I want somebody on my side about notice and pay. That's it, nothing fancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired more than anything. Relieved it's not worse, but it's not like nothing changing is good news when nothing is already a struggle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you just about cover the mortgage. In this world, what's the bill that worries you most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage, every time. Our fixed rate ends next spring and the letter says it'll go up about ninety a month, and that's ninety we haven't got unless Tom picks up more runs. We've got about three months saved, which sounds fine until the car needs a clutch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone on the farm you'd worry about, even with nothing big changing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dewi, the other hand, he's sixty-one and his knees are gone. If Gwen ever got one of those robot milkers people talk about, Dewi and me would be the ones out, plateau or no plateau. He'd never find anything else, and I'm not sure I would either.

say: I'd call AI **mostly hype** and say farms were never going to notice it.
I'd joke that the only AI on a farm is a **weather app** that's always wrong.
think: My life stays as hard as it is, because milk prices and the mortgage already squeeze us.
The Pryces are always one bad winter from **selling the herd**, AI or not.
do: Keep putting **£40 a week** into the savings tin that Tom and I agreed on.
Go to the **farmworkers' union** meeting in town I keep missing, to know my rights on notice.
feel: **Tired** more than anything, and only slightly relieved that nothing gets worse.
S0.quote: Nobody needs a computer to make milking at five in the morning any worse; milk prices and the bank manage that fine on their own.
fieldNote: Her worry here is **the mortgage**, with a fixed rate ending next spring and about ninety a month more to find.
She dismisses AI out loud, but quietly fears a **robot milker** more than any software.
Already protective of **Dewi**, the older hand, which shows her union instincts.

steps.text: Keep milking at the Pryce farm and putting £40 a week into savings
Join the farmworkers' union branch that meets in town

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office people's problem, not ours, at least at first. At work I'd tell Gwen she'd better not get ideas about replacing us. To friends I'd say the government should make the firms that profit pay for whoever gets pushed out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it starts in the paperwork and ends in the parlour. Gwen does the ordering and the records, and if a computer does those, she's got more time and money to look at machines. My job is exactly the kind of job a robot milker was built to take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start putting more aside, maybe sixty a week instead of forty, and stop the takeaway on Fridays. I'd get the union rep out to the farm to talk to Dewi and me together. And I'd write to our MP, which I've never done in my life, about protecting farm jobs if machines come in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like I'm waiting for a letter I know is coming. Not today, not this year, but I can feel it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots are slower in this one. What would you notice first on the Pryce farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the feed rep turning up with a tablet instead of a notebook, and Gwen getting that look. Then the talk at the mart about who's put a robot in, the big dairy over at Llanfair already has two. It'll be the sale-ring gossip before it's on our yard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever try any of these tools yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't think so. I've never used one of those chat things and I don't see what it would tell me that Gwen can't. Maisie could show me, she uses it for homework, but I'd rather learn the cows properly first.

say: I'd say this is **office people's** trouble first, not farm trouble.
I'd tell friends the firms that profit should **pay for** whoever gets pushed out.
think: It starts in the **paperwork** and ends in the parlour, once Gwen has time and money for machines.
My milking job is exactly what a **robot milker** was built to do.
do: Raise savings from £40 to **£60 a week** and drop the Friday takeaway.
Get the **union rep** out to the farm to talk with Dewi and me.
Write to **our MP** for the first time about protecting farm jobs.
feel: Like waiting for a **letter** she knows is coming, just not this year.
S1.quote: My job is exactly the kind of job a robot milker was built to take.
fieldNote: She sees clearly that her job is **hands-on and exposed**, even though the card says robots come slowly.
Her answer is to **organise and lobby**, not to learn the tools herself.
Turns down learning AI even with her daughter offering, a sign of her **resistance** to new tech.

steps.text: Save £60 a week instead of £40 and drop the Friday takeaway
Bring the union rep to the farm to meet Dewi and her
Write to her MP asking for rules on farm machines and jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud: this is too fast and somebody has to put the brakes on. At work I'd say Gwen and Dewi and me are in it together. Online I'd probably finally sign one of those petitions Tom's always sending me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think by 2031 I'm finished on the farm. The thinking AI in 2028 wouldn't touch the milking, but it would make Gwen's books and orders run themselves, and then three years later the robots are as good as me, and I'm not even that good yet. I'd be forty-eight with a mortgage and no trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd stop all the extras, the kids' swimming would be the hardest one to cut. I'd push the union hard to get some kind of guarantee for farm workers before 2031, and I'd go to every meeting. I'd go to Tom's mum about whether we could move in with her if it all came down, because we wouldn't be the only ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like the floor's tilting and everyone's pretending it isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Tom drives the school bus. Where does his job sit in all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom's in the same boat, or worse, because driving is half thinking and half hands. If a bus can drive itself, they'll want that before they want my milking. Two wages in our house and both of them are jobs a machine wants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Maisie and Owen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the truth, that it's going to be tight and that we stick together. Maisie's eleven, she'd see through anything else. Owen would only want to know if the dog's coming with us.

say: I'd say this is **too fast** and someone has to put the brakes on.
I'd finally sign the **petitions** Tom keeps sending me.
think: By **2031** I'm finished on the farm, because robots will match me and I'm still learning.
Both **household wages**, mine and Tom's bus driving, are jobs a machine wants.
do: Cut every extra in year one, even the kids' **swimming lessons**.
Push the **union** for a guarantee for farm workers before 2031.
Ask **Tom's mum** whether the four of us could move in if needed.
feel: **Sick**, like the floor is tilting and everyone's pretending it isn't.
S2.quote: Two wages in our house and both of them are jobs a machine wants.
fieldNote: She works out the **three-year gap** herself: paperwork goes first, then her hands-on work by 2031.
The real fear is **both incomes** going, since Tom drives the school bus.
Her plan leans on **union pressure** and family, not on new skills.

steps.text: Cancel the kids' swimming lessons and every other monthly extra
Go to every union meeting and push for a farm worker guarantee
Ask Tom's mum about moving in with her if both jobs go

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as the fast one, mostly. I'd say we've been warned, so there's no excuse for the government not having a plan. I'd be louder about it at the mart and at the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I've got a bit longer, until about 2034, before the robots can do what I do. But I don't trust myself to use the time well; I'm not one for courses and screens. I'd probably end up hoping it doesn't happen, which I know is daft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder while I still had the wage, maybe aim for six months instead of three. I'd stay in the union and get Dewi to join too. And honestly, I'd wait a year or two to see whether it's really coming before I went chasing some new job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy all the time, like a storm forecast you keep checking. But less sick than the two-year one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got five years of warning in this one. Does that change anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is time I'd use to pay down, not to learn computers. If you gave me five years' warning, I'd spend them paying off the car, not sitting in a classroom. Tom thinks I'm wrong about that, and he might be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'we stick together' before. Who else would you lean on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister in Aberbanc, the chapel crowd up the road even though I'm not a chapel person, and the union. People round here help each other when a farm goes; I've seen it with the Morgans.

say: I'd say we've been **warned**, so the government has no excuse for not having a plan.
I'd be **louder** about it at the mart and the union.
think: I've got until about **2034** before robots do my work.
I don't trust myself to use the time well, because I'm **not one for courses**.
do: Build savings from three months to **six months** while the wage lasts.
Sign **Dewi** up to the union alongside me.
**Wait a year** or two before chasing a new job.
feel: **Uneasy** all the time, like checking a storm forecast, though less sick than with two years.
S3.quote: If you gave me five years' warning, I'd spend them paying off the car, not sitting in a classroom.
fieldNote: The extra time eases the panic but not the outcome; she still expects to **lose the farm job**.
She would spend the warning **paying down debt**, not retraining, and admits Tom disagrees.
Her support network is family, neighbours and **the union**.

steps.text: Save towards six months of bills while the farm wage lasts
Get Dewi to join the farmworkers' union with her
Hold off a year or two before looking for other work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for them to sort out proper protection, so they'd better. At the union I'd want us campaigning from year one, not year nine. With friends I'd probably say I'll be retired by then, though I won't be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years plus three makes 2039, and I'd be fifty-six. That's too young to stop and too old to start again, and the mortgage still has years left on it. It's a long way off, but it's not off the table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at the Pryces' and keep the savings ticking over. I'd get involved properly in the union campaign, maybe even be the rep for our area. And I'd push the kids hard at school, because they're the ones who'll be starting out right when it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but it still sits there. Like a bill due in ten years that you can't pay off early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With a decade of warning, you'd be in your mid-fifties when robots arrive. How does that land?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fifty-six, still paying the bank, with a body that's done thirteen years of milking. At fifty-six I won't be learning to fix the robot that replaced me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the government to actually do in those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Make the firms that sell the robots pay into a fund for the people they replace, and give older workers a bridge to pension. That's not charity, that's fair. And keep some farm jobs for people, even if it costs a bit more.

say: I'd say ten years is enough for **proper protection**, so the government had better deliver.
I'd want the **union campaigning** from year one, not year nine.
think: By **2039** I'd be fifty-six, too young to stop and too old to restart.
The **mortgage** would still have years left when the robots arrive.
do: Keep working at the Pryce farm and keep the **savings** ticking over.
Stand as the **union rep** for our area.
Push Maisie and Owen hard on **school**, because they'd start work right as it lands.
feel: **Calmer**, but it sits there like a bill due in ten years.
S4.quote: At fifty-six I won't be learning to fix the robot that replaced me.
fieldNote: Ten years softens her mood but doesn't change her belief that **robots replace her** in the end.
She wants a **robot levy** fund and a bridge to pension for older workers.
Her biggest hope moves to **her children's schooling**.

steps.text: Keep milking at the Pryce farm and keep saving each week
Stand as the local farmworkers' union rep
Lobby for a fund paid by robot makers for replaced workers
Push Maisie and Owen to stay on at school and get qualifications

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028, because Tom and I would both be out inside five years with no time to do anything. What would help is a guarantee, in writing, that farm workers get paid notice and some money to tide us over, and that the companies making the robots chip in. I don't want a handout; I want the robot firms to pay their share, the same as I pay mine.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who's going to look after the animals if it goes wrong. A robot doesn't sit up with a calf at two in the morning because it's worried. Somebody should be asking that before they get rid of all of us.

headlineQuote: I don't want a handout; I want the robot firms to pay their share, the same as I pay mine.
portrait: Uma is **43**, three years into milking on the Pryce farm after the town bakery closed.
She and Tom, a **school bus driver**, cover the mortgage with about three months saved.
She **never uses AI** and would rather pay down debt than retrain.
Across the pictures her answer is **the union**, lobbying and family, not new skills.
She grows from uneasy in AI Plateau to **alarmed** in the fast AGI pictures.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her farm job and Tom's bus job could both go within five years.
whatWouldHelp: A written **guarantee** of notice and pay for farm workers, funded partly by **robot firms**.
